claim: YouTube creators receive a fixed 55% share of advertising revenue, but the absolute payout is set entirely by advertiser valuation of the audience, so per-view earnings are not a creator-controllable variable.
stance_target: The claim that creator income inequality is driven by audience commercial value rather than by content quality or effort
scope_conditions: YouTube, global platform policy as documented circa 2021-2022; documentary analysis of platform materials, not measurement of actual payouts; Western/EU authorship and framing
quoted_support: Although producers receive a set share (55%) of advertising revenue, the actual payout from content-adjacent ads depends solely on the advertisers' valuation of the parameters described.

claim: Creators serving poorer audiences or non-commercial content niches earn structurally less per view than those in commercial niches serving affluent-country audiences, because the ad auction prices audiences rather than content.
stance_target: The claim that Western creator income benchmarks cannot be transferred to Southeast Asia, because the same view count monetises at a systematically lower rate for lower-CPM audiences
scope_conditions: YouTube advertising auction; mechanism argued from documentary analysis of the ad system; the authors do NOT test or quantify the geographic implication, and no CPM figures are given
quoted_support: To earn high revenues through Google Ads, producers must try to stay within commercial niches (such as fashion or tech) and attract high-income users (either from more affluent countries or from the elite in less affluent ones), since these are valued highly by YouTube's advertisers.

claim: YouTube Select, the premium advertiser inventory tier, is restricted to the top 5% of popular channels using an undisclosed proprietary P-score, creating an explicit two-tier market in which 95% of channels are excluded from premium advertiser demand.
stance_target: The claim that platform design deliberately concentrates the highest-value revenue on a small minority of creators, structurally capping the income ceiling for the remainder
scope_conditions: YouTube, circa 2019-2022; based on Google's own public description plus secondary reporting on the P-score (Stanford 2019); ranking criteria not officially disclosed
quoted_support: YouTube Select is ostensibly exclusive to 'the top 5% of popular channels' (Google, n.d.), and while criteria for this ranking have not been communicated directly, sources indicate that a proprietary algorithm called 'P-score' plays an important role
numbers: P-score indicators: Popularity, Passion, Protection, Platform
